text: A dot-tfvars file is just a text file, and Terraform doesn't treat anything inside it specially. If a client secret ends up in one and that file gets committed, it's sitting in Git history forever, readable by anyone with repo access long after it's rotated. That's the same secrets-in-pipelines lesson this course already covered generically, now pointed squarely at Terraform: credentials come from the pipeline's own secret store, never from a file that gets committed.

The azurerm provider reads Service Principal credentials from a fixed set of environment variable names automatically, so a workflow supplies them without a single line of Terraform code changing. secrets.ARM_CLIENT_SECRET pulls from GitHub Actions secrets, configured once under repository settings, and GitHub automatically masks any secret value that happens to appear in a log. The aws provider works the same way with its own two environment variable names.

Values coming out of Terraform need the same care. Without sensitive = true on an output, a generated database password would print in plain text every single time plan or apply runs, right there in a CI log anyone with access can read. random_password generates it, and the output block's sensitive = true argument is what replaces it with the literal text sensitive in all console output instead, including the plan comment this chapter already posts on pull requests.

But that argument only changes what prints to the console and logs. The real value is still written in plain text inside the Terraform state file itself, because Terraform genuinely needs the actual value there to detect drift and plan correctly later. That's exactly why a properly secured remote backend isn't optional for anything handling real secrets — sensitive stops a password from leaking into a build log, a secured backend is what stops it from leaking out of the state file.

Credentials in through the secret store, sensitive outputs redacted from every log, state file secured at the backend — that's the full picture of keeping secrets safe in a Terraform pipeline. None of it, though, catches a different kind of problem: someone making a change by hand, outside the pipeline entirely, so the state file quietly stops matching reality. That's drift, and it's where Lesson 28 picks up.
